slot.brief: Definite integral of an odd/even function over a symmetric interval, possibly combined with a known definite-integral property like ∫f(x)dx = ∫f(a+b-x)dx to simplify before evaluating.

verdicts.working: Let f(x)=1/(1+sin x+cos x), so f(π/2−x)=f(x). Hence ∫(x+π/4)f(x)dx=(π/2)∫f(x)dx. With t=tan(x/2), ∫₀^{π/2}f(x)dx=∫₀¹dt/(1+t)=ln 2. Thus I=(π ln 2)/2.

working:
Let $J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin x+\cos x}$. Under $x\mapsto\frac{\pi}{2}-x$, the two numerators sum to $\pi$, so $2I=\pi J$. With $t=\tan\frac{x}{2}$, $J=\int_0^1\dfrac{dt}{1+t}=\ln 2$. Hence $I=\dfrac{\pi\ln 2}{2}$.

Independent check: Let f(x)=1/(1+sin x+cos x), so f(π/2−x)=f(x). Hence ∫(x+π/4)f(x)dx=(π/2)∫f(x)dx. With t=tan(x/2), ∫₀^{π/2}f(x)dx=∫₀¹dt/(1+t)=ln 2. Thus I=(π ln 2)/2.
solution:
Since $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x+\cos x}$ satisfies $f(\frac{\pi}{2}-x)=f(x)$, symmetry gives $I=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\,dx$.
Using $t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$,
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+t}=\ln 2.$$
Therefore, $I=\dfrac{\pi\ln 2}{2}$. (A)
